# UniProbe: A Learnable Token-Level Hallucination Detector for Large VLMs using Multi-Structural Internal Representations

- **Authors**: Dvir Samuel, Guy Bar-Shalom, Fabrizio Frasca, Ethan Fetaya, Yftah Ziser, Gal Chechik, Haggai Maron
- **Venue**: cs.CV
- **Published**: 2026-08-11
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10835>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.10835v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.50

## In one line

Reads a frozen vision-language model's forward pass as a structured computational trace -- a graph over image patches, query tokens and generated tokens with attention as edges, processed by interleaved relational, spatial and sequential modules -- and shows that structuring the same internals prior detectors already read lifts hallucination detection from a 69-75 AUC plateau to 90.

## Problem

Vision-language models generate content unsupported by the image, and useful mitigation needs the affected tokens located rather than the whole response discarded. The three existing approaches each pay a price: fine-tuning the model to tag hallucinated spans updates billions of parameters and can degrade the model it is meant to safeguard; training an external verifier that compares response to image requires a second vision-language model and ignores how the response was produced; and probing internal signals avoids both costs but reduces the forward pass to isolated features and hand-crafted statistics, discarding the spatial, sequential and relational structure that the computation actually has.

## Contributions

- A detector that models the forward pass as a heterogeneous computational trace -- a graph over image patches, query tokens and generated tokens with attention as edges -- rather than as isolated features or hand-crafted statistics.
- Interleaved rather than stacked structure-aware modules for relational, spatial and sequential evidence, ablated to show no single one suffices and that removing the relational graph costs most.
- The demonstration that flat probes over the same frozen internals plateau where a structured read-out does not, isolating the representation of the evidence rather than access to it as the operative variable.
- A streaming variant that detects and resamples during generation at 1.06 times vanilla latency, with a self-adaptation step addressing the distribution shift caused by different backbones hallucinating differently.
- Controls that isolate detection quality from the intervention: the same guardrail run with every competing detector, and self-adaptation applied to the strongest competitor to show adaptation alone does not explain the gain.
- Evidence that the mitigation does not work by suppression, reporting retained word count, preserved correct-object coverage, eliminated empty captions, perplexity and distribution shift alongside the hallucination reduction.
- A depth sweep showing grounding evidence concentrated in a narrow mid-network band on every backbone, with an argument for why pooling across layers dilutes rather than aggregates it.

## Method

The detector treats a single forward pass as a heterogeneous trace rather than a bag of features. A directed graph is constructed over image patches, query tokens and generated tokens with attention weights encoding the relations between them, and that trace is processed by three structure-aware modules matched to three kinds of evidence -- a graph network for relational structure, a vision transformer for two-dimensional visual geometry, and a recurrent module for response order -- interleaved rather than stacked, so spatial, relational and sequential evidence interact throughout rather than being combined at the end. The model under test stays frozen and no weights are updated. Two deployment variants follow. A streaming version detects and resamples hallucinated tokens during generation, and a self-adaptation step fine-tunes the detector on responses sampled from the target model, addressing the distribution shift that arises because different backbones hallucinate in systematically different ways so a detector trained on other models' outputs faces a train-test mismatch. Evaluation covers token-level detection against zero-shot frontier models and against trained detectors including one that fine-tunes every backbone weight, token-level localisation on a second benchmark, object-hallucination detection on self-generated captions and a heavily imbalanced probing set, and a decoding guardrail. Ablations compare flat multilayer-perceptron and transformer probes against the structured trace, remove each module in turn, sweep the read-out layer across depth, and sweep the decoding threshold.

## Results

Zero-shot prompting of frontier models is weak at fine-grained localisation (40.6 and 43.9 on the stricter token metric), and trained detectors close only part of the gap. The frozen structured read-out beats all of them on both backbones tested -- 63.2 and 52.9 against 59.1 and 49.8 for the strongest trained competitor on one backbone, 61.7 and 51.2 against 55.4 and 46.7 on the other -- which the authors note holds even though that competitor fine-tunes every backbone weight while theirs updates none, and at lower latency (1.15 times vanilla generation against 1.21 to 1.30 for the trained detectors). The object-detection result is the one that isolates the paper's claim. Every prior detector plateaus between 69 and 75 AUC on the imbalanced probing set, whether it is an external verifier or a flat hand-crafted read-out of the same frozen internals, while structuring that identical evidence as a trace reaches 90.0 -- and 92.3 F1 on self-generated captions against 82.0 for the strongest prior method. So the gain is attributed to representation of the evidence rather than to access to it. In deployment, the streaming detector cuts object-hallucination rates from 18.0 and 37.2 to 15.3 and 31.4 unadapted and to 8.2 and 16.6 after self-adaptation -- a 55 percent reduction -- at 1.06 times vanilla latency. Two controls make that readable. The same reject-and-resample guardrail is run with every competing detector, isolating detection quality from the intervention, and self-adaptation is also applied to the strongest competitor, which improves it substantially but leaves it well behind, showing adaptation alone does not explain the result. And the improvement is shown not to come from suppressing content: guarded captions retain 95.4 percent of the vanilla word count, preserve correct-object coverage, eliminate the empty captions vanilla decoding produced, and have slightly lower perplexity with a small distribution shift. The ablations are informative in two directions. Flat probes over the same signals trail the structured model by at least 30 points, and no single module suffices -- the best individually reaches 56.9 against 63.2 for the combination, with removing the relational graph costing 10.1 and removing response recurrence 4.6. The layer sweep finds detection climbing through early layers, peaking mid-network, and falling toward the output where representations specialise for next-token prediction rather than grounding, with the same shape on every backbone; reading from several layers at once consistently underperforms the single peak layer, which the authors explain as depth pooling diluting a narrow band with early generic features and late prediction-specific ones, aggravated by varying activation scales biasing naive averaging toward high-norm layers. The threshold sweep reports the trade rather than only the chosen point: a more aggressive setting cuts hallucination a further 36 percent while removing 12 percent of correct mentions.

## Limitations

Stated where it matters. The read-out layer is chosen per backbone on validation data, so it is a tuned hyperparameter rather than a constant, and the paper reports that multi-layer pooling underperforms rather than presenting the single-layer choice as obviously right. The decoding threshold is likewise selected as the most aggressive setting that does not remove correct content, with the cost of a more aggressive one quantified. Self-adaptation requires sampling from the target model, so a deployed detector is model-specific and has to be re-adapted per backbone. Not stated but worth noticing: the detector is trained supervised on hallucination labels, so it is a learned classifier over internal states rather than an interpretability result about how grounding is represented -- the layer sweep is suggestive about where grounding lives but the model is optimised for detection, not for locating a mechanism. The comparison against a fine-tuned competitor is favourable but that competitor is also solving a different problem, since fine-tuning changes the model while this leaves it frozen. And the object-hallucination gains are largest on a benchmark the authors describe as heavily imbalanced, where AUC and F1 can move a great deal on relatively few decisions.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: Two results here bear directly on how this archive reads probing evidence. The first is a controlled attribution that is rare and clean: every prior detector -- external verifiers and flat hand-crafted read-outs of the same frozen internals alike -- plateaus between 69 and 75 AUC on one benchmark, and structuring that identical evidence as a graph over patches, query tokens and generated tokens reaches 90. Nothing about access to the model changed; only the representation of the evidence did. That is a direct challenge to the archive's implicit default of scoring an internal signal with a linear probe over pooled activations, and the flat-probe ablation makes the point again from the other side, trailing the structured model by at least 30 points on the same signals. Where a linear probe underperforms, the correct inference may be that the evidence is relational or sequential rather than that it is absent. The second is a depth result that pairs with material the archive already holds. Detection climbs through early layers, peaks mid-network, and falls toward the output where representations specialise for next-token prediction rather than grounding -- the same shape on every backbone tested -- and reading from several layers at once consistently underperforms the single peak, because pooling dilutes a narrow band with early generic features and late prediction-specific ones while varying activation scales bias naive averaging toward high-norm layers. That is a concrete argument against layer-pooled probes, and it sits alongside the archive's other evidence that the useful band is narrow, model-specific, and not where a hand-picked fraction of depth would put it. Two cautions on how far to read the interpretability claim. This is a supervised detector optimised for detection, not an analysis of how grounding is computed, so the layer profile locates where a classifier finds signal rather than where the model does the work. And the paper's own discipline on the mitigation side is worth borrowing regardless: it runs the same guardrail with every competing detector to isolate detection quality from the intervention, applies its self-adaptation step to the strongest competitor to show adaptation is not the explanation, and reports word count, correct-object coverage, perplexity and distribution shift to establish that the improvement is not suppression.

## Abstract

Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve impressive visual reasoning and dialogue capabilities, yet frequently hallucinate content unsupported by the visual input. Effective mitigation requires token-level localization, enabling targeted intervention without discarding the entire response. Existing detectors require expensive full-model fine-tuning, rely on external verifiers that ignore the model's generation process, or reduce internal signals to isolated features and hand-crafted statistics, discarding spatial, sequential, and relational structure. We introduce \textbf{UniProbe}, a lightweight, unified, learnable detector that models a frozen LVLM's heterogeneous computational trace from a single forward pass. UniProbe constructs a directed graph over image patches, query tokens, and generated tokens, with attention weights encoding their relations. It processes this trace with alternating structure-aware modules: a GNN for relational evidence, a ViT for 2-D visual geometry, and a GRU for response order. Interleaving them allows spatial, relational, and sequential evidence to interact throughout the detector. We further develop a streaming variant for hallucination-aware decoding, which detects and resamples hallucinated tokens during generation, and a self-adaptation strategy aligning the detector with the LVLM's own generations. Across diverse LVLM backbones, UniProbe achieves state-of-the-art token-level and object-hallucination detection. During decoding, it reduces object hallucinations by up to 55\% at $1.06\times$ the latency of standard generation.
